options.a: Greater than 20 kHz (above human hearing)
options.b: Less than 20 Hz (below human hearing)
options.c: Between 20 Hz and 20 kHz (audible range)
options.d: Greater than 2 MHz (the diagnostic range)

distractorExplanations.b: Sound below 20 Hz is infrasound; ultrasound is the opposite end, above the upper limit of hearing.
distractorExplanations.c: 20 Hz to 20 kHz is audible sound; ultrasound begins above 20 kHz.
distractorExplanations.d: About 2 MHz is the low end of typical diagnostic imaging; the definition of ultrasound starts at 20 kHz.

options.a: Propagation speed times frequency (c × f)
options.b: Propagation speed divided by frequency (c/f)
options.c: Frequency divided by propagation speed (f/c)
options.d: Spatial pulse length times number of cycles

distractorExplanations.a: Multiplying speed by frequency gives the wrong units; wavelength is speed divided by frequency (λ = c/f).
distractorExplanations.c: That inverts the ratio; f/c equals 1/λ, so higher frequency would wrongly give a longer wavelength.
distractorExplanations.d: SPL equals cycles × wavelength, so wavelength is SPL divided by the number of cycles, not multiplied by it.

options.a: The transducer's operating frequency
options.b: The amplitude and intensity of the pulse
options.c: Medium stiffness (elasticity) and density
options.d: Pulse repetition frequency and depth setting

distractorExplanations.a: Frequency is set by the source; speed is a property of the medium and is the same for all frequencies in soft tissue.
distractorExplanations.b: Amplitude and intensity describe the strength of the wave; they do not change how fast sound travels in a medium.
distractorExplanations.d: PRF and depth control pulse timing on the machine; the medium's stiffness and density set propagation speed.

options.a: Frequency × wavelength
options.b: Density divided by propagation speed
options.c: Stiffness × propagation speed
options.d: Density × propagation speed

distractorExplanations.b: Dividing inverts the relationship; impedance is density multiplied by propagation speed (Z = ρc, in rayls).
distractorExplanations.c: Stiffness and density together set propagation speed; impedance uses density times speed, not stiffness.
distractorExplanations.a: Fλ = c.

options.a: Reciprocals (T = 1/f)
options.b: Directly proportional (T ∝ f)
options.c: Set by the medium
options.d: Related by the speed (T = c/f)

distractorExplanations.b: As frequency rises the period gets shorter, so the two are inversely related, not directly proportional.
distractorExplanations.c: The sound source (transducer) sets both period and frequency; the medium sets propagation speed.
distractorExplanations.d: Speed divided by frequency gives wavelength (λ = c/f); period is simply the reciprocal of frequency.

options.a: Linear: 3 dB ≈ factor of 3; 10 dB ≈ factor of 10
options.b: Logarithmic: 3 dB ≈ factor of 2; 10 dB ≈ factor of 100
options.c: An absolute unit of intensity in W/cm²
options.d: Logarithmic: 3 dB ≈ factor of 2; 10 dB ≈ factor of 10

distractorExplanations.a: The dB scale is logarithmic, not linear; +3 dB doubles intensity rather than tripling it.
distractorExplanations.b: 3 dB does double intensity, but 10 dB is a factor of 10; a factor of 100 is 20 dB.
distractorExplanations.c: Decibels express a relative ratio; W/cm² is the absolute unit of intensity, not the dB scale.

options.a: The interface is large and smooth relative to wavelength
options.b: Scatterers are much smaller than wavelength only (Rayleigh)
options.c: The interface is rough and irregular relative to wavelength
options.d: Impedances on both sides of the boundary are equal

distractorExplanations.c: Rough, irregular interfaces cause diffuse scattering (backscatter) in many directions, not specular reflection.
distractorExplanations.d: With equal impedances there is no mismatch, so no reflection of any kind occurs at the boundary.
distractorExplanations.b: Rayleigh is small scatterers.

options.a: Reflection—the angle of reflection equals incidence
options.b: Refraction—bending of the beam across an oblique interface
options.c: Attenuation—loss of beam intensity with depth and frequency
options.d: Scattering—redirection of sound by small reflectors

distractorExplanations.a: Equal angles of incidence and reflection is the law of reflection; Snell's law governs the transmitted (refracted) beam.
distractorExplanations.c: Attenuation describes energy loss with depth and frequency; Snell's law describes the change in beam direction.
distractorExplanations.d: Scattering from small or rough reflectors is not described by Snell's law, which relates angles to speed ratios.

ardms-spi-readiness-check-physics-basics.explanation: Refraction can laterally displace structures (e.g., edge artifacts/duodenum-type teaching cases); it bends the beam when speed changes across an oblique interface.

options.a: Amplitude squared
options.b: Amplitude cubed
options.c: Wavelength squared
options.d: Square root of power

distractorExplanations.b: Intensity scales with the square of amplitude, so doubling amplitude quadruples intensity, not an eightfold rise.
distractorExplanations.c: Wavelength affects resolution and attenuation; intensity depends on amplitude squared, not wavelength.
distractorExplanations.d: Intensity is power divided by beam area, so it is directly proportional to power, not to its square root.

ardms-spi-readiness-check-physics-basics.explanation: Acoustic intensity relates to amplitude squared (power/area considerations) for a given medium relationship.

options.a: Hits a boundary at 90° between media with different speeds
options.b: Obliquely encounters media with different propagation speeds
options.c: Obliquely meets media with different impedances but equal speeds
options.d: Passes through a single uniform medium at a steady speed

distractorExplanations.a: At normal (90°) incidence there is no refraction even when speeds differ; obliquity is required.
distractorExplanations.c: An impedance mismatch alone causes reflection; refraction requires a difference in propagation speeds.
distractorExplanations.d: With no boundary and no speed change there is nothing to bend the beam, so refraction cannot occur.

options.a: Absolute beam intensity measured in watts per square centimeter
options.b: Relative changes in intensity or amplitude on a logarithmic scale
options.c: Changes in pulse frequency expressed on a linear kilohertz scale
options.d: The depth of a reflector calculated from echo return time

distractorExplanations.a: W/cm² is the absolute unit of intensity; decibels express relative ratios, not absolute values.
distractorExplanations.c: Frequency is measured in hertz; decibels are logarithmic ratios of intensity or amplitude, not frequency.
distractorExplanations.d: Reflector depth comes from the range equation (13 µs per cm round trip), not from decibel measurements.

options.a: Certain materials convert pressure to electricity and vice versa
options.b: Electric current heats a crystal, which then emits sound
options.c: Magnetic fields make the crystal change shape to emit sound
options.d: Materials convert electricity to pressure but not the reverse

distractorExplanations.b: Heating does not produce the ultrasound pulse; voltage deforms the crystal directly, and heat can destroy it above the Curie point.
distractorExplanations.c: Shape change driven by a magnetic field is magnetostriction, not the piezoelectric effect, which uses voltage.
distractorExplanations.d: The effect is reciprocal: the same element converts voltage to pressure on transmit and pressure to voltage on receive.

options.a: Shorten the pulse by absorbing the crystal's ringing
options.b: Improve transmission between PZT and tissue
options.c: Focus the beam in the elevation plane
options.d: Raise the impedance above that of PZT

distractorExplanations.a: Absorbing ringing to shorten the pulse is the job of the backing (damping) material behind the crystal.
distractorExplanations.c: Elevational focusing is done by the acoustic lens, not by the matching layer.
distractorExplanations.d: The matching layer impedance sits between PZT and skin; raising it above PZT would increase reflection.

ardms-spi-readiness-check-transducers-be.explanation: The matching layer has an impedance between PZT and tissue, improving transmission; its thickness is about 1/4 wavelength.

options.a: Increases ringing to raise the quality factor (Q)
options.b: Improves lateral resolution by narrowing the beam width
options.c: Shortens spatial pulse length improving axial resolution
options.d: Increases sensitivity by lengthening the transmitted pulse

distractorExplanations.a: Damping reduces ringing and lowers Q (wider bandwidth); higher Q belongs to lightly damped CW transducers.
distractorExplanations.b: Beam width and lateral resolution are improved by focusing, not by the backing material.
distractorExplanations.d: Damping shortens the pulse and actually reduces sensitivity; it does not lengthen the pulse.

ardms-spi-readiness-check-transducers-be.explanation: Low-Q damped transducers are used for imaging; continuous wave Doppler is lightly damped. Damping shortens SPL at the cost of sensitivity.

options.a: Narrower beam width at the focus
options.b: Lower transducer frequency
options.c: More cycles in the pulse
options.d: Shorter spatial pulse length

distractorExplanations.a: Beam width governs lateral resolution; axial resolution depends on spatial pulse length.
distractorExplanations.b: Lower frequency means longer wavelength and longer SPL, which worsens axial resolution.
distractorExplanations.c: More cycles lengthen SPL.

ardms-spi-readiness-check-transducers-be.explanation: AR ≈ SPL/2; fewer cycles and shorter λ help, so higher frequency and more damping improve axial resolution.

options.a: Focus (narrowest beam width)
options.b: Far (Fraunhofer) zone
options.c: Transducer face, near the crystal
options.d: Deepest part of the image

distractorExplanations.b: The beam diverges in the far zone, so lateral resolution degrades beyond the focus.
distractorExplanations.c: At the face the beam is as wide as the crystal, about twice its width at the focus.
distractorExplanations.d: The deepest region is in the diverging far field, where beam width and lateral resolution are worst.

options.a: Steering one beam with phased delays from all elements
options.b: Firing groups of elements in sequence across the face
options.c: Rotating a single element with a motor inside the probe
options.d: Firing every element together as one large crystal

distractorExplanations.a: Steering with phased time delays from a small footprint produces a sector image, which is a phased array.
distractorExplanations.c: A motor-driven single element is an older mechanical sector transducer, not a linear sequenced array.
distractorExplanations.d: Firing all elements at once makes one wide unsteered beam; linear arrays build lines by firing small groups in turn.

options.a: A motor that rotates a single crystal
options.b: Firing element groups in sequence along the face
options.c: Minute time delays (phasing) across elements
options.d: A curved face that spreads the scan lines

distractorExplanations.a: A rotating crystal describes a mechanical sector transducer; phased arrays steer electronically.
distractorExplanations.b: Sequential firing of element groups is how linear sequenced arrays make rectangular images.
distractorExplanations.d: A curved face produces the blunted sector of a convex array; phased arrays steer with timing delays.

ardms-spi-readiness-check-transducers-be.explanation: Electronic beam forming with minute time delays steers/focuses the beam, enabling sector imaging from small probes (cardiac).

options.a: Increasing output power and overall receiver gain
options.b: Wider element spacing across a larger total aperture
options.c: Lowering the frame rate with more transmit foci
options.d: Apodization, subdicing, and tight element spacing

distractorExplanations.a: More power and gain raise lobe energy along with the main beam; they do not suppress grating lobes.
distractorExplanations.b: Wider element spacing makes grating lobes worse; elements should be spaced closely (about half a wavelength).
distractorExplanations.c: More transmit foci improve lateral resolution across depth but do not address grating lobes.

options.a: Pulse duration divided by pulse repetition period
options.b: Pulse repetition period divided by the pulse duration
options.c: Pulse duration multiplied by the frame rate
options.d: Pulse duration divided by the wave period

distractorExplanations.b: That inverts the ratio and would give values above 1; duty factor is PD/PRP, a fraction of time transmitting.
distractorExplanations.c: Frame rate is not the pulse repetition frequency; duty factor uses PD × PRF (equivalently PD/PRP).
distractorExplanations.d: Pulse duration divided by the wave period gives the number of cycles in the pulse, not duty factor.

ardms-spi-readiness-check-transducers-be.explanation: DF is unitless (the fraction of time transmitting); CW Doppler DF = 1; imaging DF is very small.

options.a: Number of cycles × period
options.b: Number of cycles × wavelength
options.c: Wavelength ÷ number of cycles
options.d: Propagation speed ÷ frequency (c/f)

distractorExplanations.a: Cycles multiplied by period gives pulse duration (a time), not spatial pulse length (a distance).
distractorExplanations.c: SPL grows with more cycles, so it is wavelength multiplied by cycles, not divided.
distractorExplanations.d: c/f equals one wavelength; SPL is that wavelength multiplied by the number of cycles in the pulse.

options.a: Conversion between electrical energy and mechanical energy
options.b: Conversion of electrical energy into heat within the crystal
options.c: Conversion between light and sound energy in crystals
options.d: Conversion of magnetic energy into sound in the probe

distractorExplanations.b: Heat is an unwanted by-product; the piezoelectric effect converts voltage into mechanical vibration and back.
distractorExplanations.c: Light-to-sound conversion is the photoacoustic effect, not piezoelectricity.
distractorExplanations.d: Magnetic-to-mechanical conversion is magnetostriction; piezoelectric crystals respond to voltage.

ardms-spi-readiness-check-transducers-be.explanation: Piezoelectric materials expand/contract with voltage and generate voltage from pressure, converting between electrical and mechanical (sound) energy in crystals.

options.a: Improves lateral resolution at multiple depths but can reduce frame rate
options.b: Improves lateral resolution at multiple depths and raises frame rate
options.c: Improves axial resolution at multiple depths but reduces frame rate
options.d: Reduces frame rate without changing lateral resolution

distractorExplanations.b: Each extra focus needs another transmit pulse per line, so frame rate falls rather than rises.
distractorExplanations.c: Focusing narrows beam width, which affects lateral resolution; axial resolution depends on SPL.
distractorExplanations.d: Frame rate does fall, but the purpose and effect of extra foci is better lateral resolution over depth.

options.a: Number of cycles in the pulse × wavelength
options.b: Number of cycles in the pulse × period
options.c: Pulse duration × pulse repetition frequency
options.d: One half of the axial resolution value

distractorExplanations.b: Cycles times period is pulse duration, the time version; SPL uses wavelength to give a distance.
distractorExplanations.c: Pulse duration times PRF equals duty factor, not spatial pulse length.
distractorExplanations.d: Axial resolution is SPL/2, so SPL is twice the axial resolution, not half of it.

options.a: A pie-shaped sector that converges to a tiny footprint
options.b: Blunted-sector shaped with a wider field at depth
options.c: Rectangular with a constant width at depth
options.d: Trapezoidal from steering a flat linear face

distractorExplanations.a: A pointed sector from a small footprint is the phased-array format; convex arrays have a broad curved top.
distractorExplanations.c: A rectangle of constant width is produced by a linear sequenced array, not a curved array.
distractorExplanations.d: A trapezoid comes from steering the outer lines of a flat linear array (virtual convex), not a curved face.

ardms-spi-readiness-check-transducers-be.explanation: Curved arrays create blunted sector formats common in abdominal imaging, from sequential firing along a curved face.

options.a: The range of frequencies in the pulse
options.b: The main (resonant) frequency of the crystal
options.c: The number of pulses sent per second
options.d: The width of the beam at the focus

distractorExplanations.b: The resonant frequency is the center or operating frequency; bandwidth is the spread of frequencies around it.
distractorExplanations.c: Pulses per second is the pulse repetition frequency, a timing setting unrelated to bandwidth.
distractorExplanations.d: Beam width at the focus governs lateral resolution; bandwidth is a frequency range, not a dimension.

ardms-spi-readiness-check-transducers-be.explanation: Bandwidth is the range of frequencies in the transmitted/received pulse; broader bandwidth (more damping) shortens pulses and improves axial resolution.

options.a: Reflector speed, the cosine of the Doppler angle, and operating frequency
options.b: Reflector speed, the sine of the Doppler angle, and operating frequency
options.c: Reflector speed and operating frequency, but not the Doppler angle
options.d: The pulse repetition frequency and the depth of the sample gate

distractorExplanations.b: The Doppler equation uses cosine, which is maximal at 0°; sine would wrongly make the shift maximal at 90°.
distractorExplanations.c: The shift depends on cos θ, so the angle matters and must be corrected for velocity estimates.
distractorExplanations.d: PRF and gate depth set the Nyquist limit and range, not the magnitude of the Doppler shift itself.

options.a: Cosine is 1 so the Doppler shift is maximal
options.b: Cosine is 0 so no Doppler shift is detected
options.c: Cosine is 0.5 so the shift is halved
options.d: Velocity estimates are at their most accurate

distractorExplanations.a: Cos θ equals 1 at 0°, where the shift is maximal; at 90° cosine is 0.
distractorExplanations.c: Cos θ equals 0.5 at 60°; at 90° it is 0 and no shift is detected.
distractorExplanations.d: Angles near 90° give the largest velocity errors; keep the angle at or below 60° for velocity estimates.

options.a: The wall filter is set too high for slow flow
options.b: CW Doppler is used (CW aliases the same way)
options.c: Nyquist limit is exceeded (shift > PRF/2)
options.d: The Doppler shift is below PRF/2

distractorExplanations.a: A high wall filter removes low-velocity signals near the baseline; it does not cause wraparound aliasing.
distractorExplanations.d: A shift below PRF/2 is under the Nyquist limit and is displayed correctly; aliasing needs a shift above it.
distractorExplanations.b: CW does not alias the same (no PRF sampling limit).

options.a: 4v^2 (modified Bernoulli)
options.b: 4v (peak velocity × 4)
options.c: v^2/4 (velocity squared over 4)
options.d: 8v^2 (doubled for valves)

distractorExplanations.b: The velocity must be squared; ΔP = 4v², so 4 m/s gives 64 mmHg, not 16 mmHg.
distractorExplanations.c: The factor 4 multiplies v², it does not divide it; ΔP = 4v² in mmHg with v in m/s.
distractorExplanations.d: The simplified constant is 4, not 8; there is no doubling for valves in the modified Bernoulli equation.

options.a: Pressure drop across a stenotic valve
options.b: Tendency for laminar vs turbulent flow
options.c: Volume flow rate through a vessel
options.d: Maximum velocity before aliasing occurs

distractorExplanations.a: Pressure drop across a stenosis is estimated with the Bernoulli equation, not the Reynolds number.
distractorExplanations.c: Volume flow is described by Poiseuille's law (Q = ΔP/R), not by the Reynolds number.
distractorExplanations.d: The maximum unaliased velocity is set by the Nyquist limit (PRF/2), not by the Reynolds number.

options.a: Larger packets improve velocity estimates and raise frame rate
options.b: Smaller packets improve sensitivity but reduce frame rate
options.c: Larger packets improve velocity estimates but reduce frame rate
options.d: Larger packets reduce aliasing by raising the color Nyquist limit

distractorExplanations.a: Each extra pulse per line takes time, so larger packets lower the frame rate.
distractorExplanations.b: Smaller packets raise frame rate but reduce sensitivity and velocity accuracy; the tradeoff is reversed.
distractorExplanations.d: The Nyquist limit depends on PRF, not packet size; larger packets do not reduce aliasing.

options.a: Strength/amplitude of Doppler shifts
options.b: Mean velocity and direction of flow
options.c: Peak velocity over time as a spectrum
options.d: Tissue motion rather than blood flow

distractorExplanations.b: Mean velocity and direction are what color (velocity) Doppler maps; power Doppler shows signal strength.
distractorExplanations.c: A velocity-time spectrum is the spectral Doppler display, not power Doppler.
distractorExplanations.d: Low-velocity, high-amplitude tissue motion is displayed by tissue Doppler imaging, not power Doppler.

ardms-spi-readiness-check-doppler-hemody.explanation: Power Doppler displays signal strength rather than mean velocity/direction; it is more sensitive to flow presence and less angle dependent than color.

options.a: Plug flow sampled with a small gate volume
options.b: Turbulent flow or large sample volume
options.c: A Doppler angle of exactly 0°
options.d: Aliasing from too low a PRF

distractorExplanations.a: Plug flow with a small gate has a narrow velocity range and a clear spectral window, the opposite of broadening.
distractorExplanations.c: A 0° angle maximizes the shift and minimizes geometric broadening; it does not cause spectral fill-in.
distractorExplanations.d: Aliasing wraps the peak velocities around the baseline; it does not fill in the spectral window.

ardms-spi-readiness-check-doppler-hemody.explanation: Fill-in of the spectral window suggests turbulence or technical factors, such as a large sample volume encompassing varied velocities.

options.a: Shows flow direction and mean velocity more accurately than color Doppler
options.b: Is more sensitive to low flow and less angle-dependent than velocity color Doppler
options.c: Is less prone to flash artifact and has a higher frame rate than color Doppler
options.d: Measures peak velocities for stenosis grading without angle correction

distractorExplanations.a: Power Doppler does not display direction or velocity magnitude; that is the strength of color and spectral Doppler.
distractorExplanations.c: Power Doppler is more prone to flash (motion) artifact and usually has a lower frame rate than color Doppler.
distractorExplanations.d: Stenosis grading needs angle-corrected spectral velocities; power Doppler gives no velocity values.

ardms-spi-readiness-check-doppler-hemody.explanation: Power Doppler encodes strength of the Doppler signal; it is relatively angle-insensitive compared with color velocity maps and does not show direction/velocity magnitude the same way.

options.a: Chaotic multidirectional velocities filling the spectrum at rest
options.b: Streamlined layers with a relatively narrow range of velocities
options.c: Fastest layers at the walls and slowest layers in the center
options.d: Flow that reverses direction in every cardiac cycle

distractorExplanations.c: In laminar (parabolic) flow the fastest layers are in the center and the slowest are at the walls.
distractorExplanations.d: Flow reversal (as in triphasic arterial flow) can occur with laminar flow but does not define it.
distractorExplanations.a: Not the best answer here; the right answer is “Streamlined layers with a relatively narrow range of velocities in a vessel”.

options.a: The Nyquist limit at any given depth
options.b: Which portion of the vessel is interrogated
options.c: The Doppler angle used for velocity correction
options.d: The transmitted frequency of the Doppler beam

distractorExplanations.a: The Nyquist limit depends on PRF, which is set by gate depth, not by gate size.
distractorExplanations.c: The Doppler angle is set by beam steering and the angle cursor, not by the size of the sample gate.
distractorExplanations.d: The transmitted frequency is chosen on the transducer; gate size does not change it.

ardms-spi-readiness-check-doppler-hemody.explanation: Larger gates include more of the vessel and more velocity components, which can increase spectral broadening.

options.a: Estimate mean Doppler shifts rapidly across many gates
options.b: Display the full velocity spectrum at a single gate
options.c: Estimate peak Doppler shifts using fast Fourier transform
options.d: Suppress wall motion clutter from the color image

distractorExplanations.b: Displaying the full spectrum at one gate is spectral Doppler, which uses FFT rather than autocorrelation.
distractorExplanations.c: FFT is the processing method for spectral Doppler; color Doppler uses autocorrelation to estimate mean shifts.
distractorExplanations.d: Clutter from wall motion is removed by the wall (clutter) filter, not by autocorrelation.

ardms-spi-readiness-check-doppler-hemody.explanation: Color flow uses autocorrelation (or similar) for fast mean-velocity estimates across many gates for the color display.

options.a: Highly attenuating/reflecting structures
options.b: Fluid-filled simple cysts and the bladder
options.c: Areas where far-field TGC is set too high
options.d: Tissues with lower propagation speed than 1540

distractorExplanations.b: Low-attenuating fluid such as cysts and the bladder produces enhancement, the opposite of shadowing.
distractorExplanations.c: Excess far-field TGC makes deep tissue too bright; it does not create an acoustic shadow.
distractorExplanations.d: Speed differences cause range (depth) errors and refraction, not shadowing distal to a structure.

ardms-spi-readiness-check-artifacts-safe.explanation: Useful diagnostically for stones; distinguish from improper TGC. Shadows form deep to calcifications, stones and bone.

options.a: Gallstones and renal calculi
options.b: Low-attenuating fluid (cysts, bladder)
options.c: Calcified arterial plaque
options.d: Dense solid masses that absorb most of the beam

distractorExplanations.a: Stones are highly attenuating and cast shadows, not enhancement.
distractorExplanations.c: Calcified plaque reflects and attenuates strongly, producing a shadow rather than enhancement.
distractorExplanations.d: Highly attenuating solid masses cause shadowing; enhancement occurs deep to low-attenuating fluid.

options.a: A duplicate structure deep to a strong curved reflector
options.b: Dark bands distal to a highly attenuating structure
options.c: Multiple equally spaced echoes at increasing depths
options.d: A structure displaced sideways at an oblique interface

distractorExplanations.a: A duplicate image deep to a strong curved reflector such as the diaphragm is mirror-image artifact.
distractorExplanations.b: Dark bands distal to an attenuating structure are acoustic shadowing, not reverberation.
distractorExplanations.d: Sideways displacement at an oblique interface is a refraction artifact.

ardms-spi-readiness-check-artifacts-safe.explanation: Reverberation produces multiple equally spaced echoes from strong parallel reflectors; comet-tail/ring-down are related variants taught in SPI.

options.a: Simple cysts with posterior enhancement
options.b: Small calcifications causing comet tails
options.c: Curved cyst edges that bend the beam
options.d: Strong reflectors like diaphragm/pleura

distractorExplanations.a: Posterior enhancement deep to cysts is a through-transmission artifact, not a mirror image.
distractorExplanations.b: Comet tails from small calcifications or metal are a reverberation artifact, not mirror image.
distractorExplanations.c: Beam bending at curved cyst edges produces edge (refraction) shadows, not a duplicated structure.

ardms-spi-readiness-check-artifacts-safe.explanation: Strong reflectors like the diaphragm/pleura create a duplicated structure; liver lesions can appear mirrored into the lung base.

options.a: False echoes that appear to originate from the main beam path
options.b: Multiple equally spaced echoes from parallel reflectors
options.c: False Doppler signals but no effect on the grayscale B-mode image
options.d: Duplicated structures deep to the diaphragm

distractorExplanations.b: Equally spaced echoes from parallel reflectors are reverberation, not side- or grating-lobe artifact.
distractorExplanations.c: Lobe artifacts affect both B-mode and Doppler, placing off-axis echoes as if they were on the beam axis.
distractorExplanations.d: A duplicated structure deep to the diaphragm is mirror-image artifact, not a lobe artifact.

options.a: Use the lowest output possible even if images are nondiagnostic
options.b: Use output exposures As Low As Reasonably Achievable
options.c: Keep exposure below a fixed legal dose limit per exam
options.d: Track cumulative ionizing dose as with CT

distractorExplanations.a: ALARA balances exposure against diagnostic quality; a nondiagnostic exam is not reasonable and may need repeating.
distractorExplanations.c: ALARA is a judgment principle, not a per-exam dose limit; diagnostic ultrasound has no ionizing dose to cap.
distractorExplanations.d: Ultrasound is non-ionizing, so there is no cumulative ionizing dose to track as with CT.

ardms-spi-readiness-check-artifacts-safe.explanation: Use output exposures As Low As Reasonably Achievable for diagnostic quality. Monitor MI/TI; reduce power, dwell time, and use appropriate modes.

options.a: Heating of fetal bone
options.b: Aliasing at high PRF
options.c: Cavitation bioeffects
options.d: Ionizing DNA damage

distractorExplanations.a: Bone heating is estimated by the thermal index for bone (TIB), not the mechanical index.
distractorExplanations.b: Aliasing is a Doppler sampling artifact related to low PRF, not a bioeffect indexed by MI.
distractorExplanations.d: Ultrasound is non-ionizing; MI relates to mechanical effects such as cavitation, not ionizing damage.

options.a: Likelihood of cavitation from peak rarefactional pressure
options.b: The exact measured temperature rise in tissue
options.c: Cumulative ionizing dose to the fetus
options.d: Potential tissue heating from ultrasound absorption

distractorExplanations.a: Cavitation likelihood from peak rarefactional pressure is described by the mechanical index (MI), not TI.
distractorExplanations.b: TI is a modeled ratio of output power to the power needed to raise tissue 1°C, not a measured temperature.
distractorExplanations.c: Ultrasound is non-ionizing; TI estimates heating, not radiation dose.

options.a: Echoes from deep structures return after the next pulse is sent
options.b: Sound travels slower than the assumed 1540 m/s in tissue
options.c: Echoes bounce repeatedly between two strong parallel reflectors
options.d: The pulse repetition period is much longer than the echo time

distractorExplanations.b: A slower actual speed causes a speed (range) error that places reflectors too deep, not range ambiguity.
distractorExplanations.c: Repeated bouncing between parallel reflectors is reverberation artifact.
distractorExplanations.d: A long PRP lets all echoes return before the next pulse, which prevents range ambiguity.

ardms-spi-readiness-check-artifacts-safe.explanation: Range ambiguity occurs when the PRP is too short; reduce it by lowering PRF/scale or adjusting depth/timing expectations.

options.a: The spectral window due to turbulent flow
options.b: Anechoic structures with false echoes
options.c: Acoustic shadows distal to calcifications
options.d: Gaps between scan lines in the far field

distractorExplanations.a: Spectral window fill-in comes from turbulence or a large gate, not from slice thickness.
distractorExplanations.c: Shadows deep to calcifications are attenuation artifacts; slice thickness adds echoes to anechoic areas.
distractorExplanations.d: Gaps between far-field lines relate to line density, not to beam thickness in the elevation plane.

ardms-spi-readiness-check-artifacts-safe.explanation: False echoes from beam elevation thickness fill in anechoic structures; elevational focusing/1.5D arrays reduce slice thickness artifacts.

options.a: Reverberation from closely spaced strong reflectors
options.b: Refraction at the edges of curved structures
options.c: Mirror imaging across a strong reflector like the diaphragm
options.d: Propagation speed error from passing through fat

distractorExplanations.b: Refraction at curved edges produces edge shadows, not the tapering echo trail of a comet tail.
distractorExplanations.c: A duplicated structure across the diaphragm is mirror-image artifact, not comet tail.
distractorExplanations.d: Slower speed in fat causes range errors and displacement, not a dense trail of reverberation echoes.

options.a: PRF is so high that deep echoes return after the next pulse is sent
options.b: PRF is so low that echoes return long before the next pulse is sent
options.c: Sound reflects back and forth between two strong parallel interfaces
options.d: Sound speed in the tissue is lower than the assumed 1540 m/s

distractorExplanations.b: A low PRF gives a long listening time, so every echo returns before the next pulse; that prevents range ambiguity.
distractorExplanations.c: Back-and-forth reflection between parallel interfaces is reverberation artifact.
distractorExplanations.d: A lower actual speed causes a range (speed) error that displays reflectors too deep, not range ambiguity.

options.a: Distal to the edges of a curved structure such as a cyst
options.b: Distal to a gallstone with strong central attenuation
options.c: Deep to a fluid-filled cyst as a bright band
options.d: Proximal to the near wall of a vessel as equally spaced lines

distractorExplanations.b: Shadowing deep to a gallstone is an attenuation shadow from the stone itself, not a refraction edge shadow.
distractorExplanations.c: A bright band deep to a cyst is posterior acoustic enhancement, not edge shadowing.
distractorExplanations.d: Equally spaced lines near a vessel wall are reverberation artifact, not a refraction shadow.

options.a: Use the lowest power setting even when images become nondiagnostic
options.b: Minimize output and exposure time while obtaining diagnostic images
options.c: Raise output power first, then reduce receiver gain to compensate
options.d: Monitor MI only, since heating is not a concern in obstetrics

distractorExplanations.a: ALARA still requires diagnostic images; a nondiagnostic scan adds repeat exposure without benefit.
distractorExplanations.c: ALARA calls for increasing receiver gain first and output power only if needed, the reverse order.
distractorExplanations.d: Fetal bone heating makes TI (especially TIB) a key concern in obstetrics, so MI alone is not enough.
